items.title: UbuTube
items.date: UbuWeb, reimagined as a streaming platform.

description: UbuWeb (ubu.com) is a digital avant-garde media library founded in 1996. Notoriously untethered from capital and legal flows, UbuWeb is 'a purposely unstable library, a conflicted curation, an archive assembled by embracing the fragmented, the biased, the subjective, and the incomplete.'[2]

UbuTube's conduct and development over the last thirty years has been admirably reflective of its mission. Its hundreds of thousands of files remain freely and readily accessible to all. However, as anticipated by its creators, some parts of the site have not withstood the test of time. Links are broken, file types are unsupported, and content is unorganized. Given the importance of UbuWeb's work and my particular affinity for avant-garde film, I took to preserving the site through my own guerilla archivism. The result was UbuTube, a reimagining of UbuWeb that aims to provide a formal, consistent backdrop for UbuWeb's disparate catalog.

UbuTube operates on axioms of minimalism, immediacy, and universality, but also provides its users with a hightened degree of personalization and interactivity. None of the original content has been altered, but the container has been radically changed.

srcs.caption: Side-by-side comparison of an UbuWeb film page with its corresponding UbuTube page.[1]

description: In order to isomorphically translate UbuWeb's data to UbuTube, the archive must be archived. The UbuTube crawler scrapes UbuWeb's 3000+ film and artist pages from on a pruned list of URLs. The UbuTube parser takes that content, removes extraneous HTML, and preserves it in a database. Film objects are linked to artist objects based on authorship.

The biggest challenge during development came when trying to accurately sanitize the original pages. While many pages on ubu.com share the same format, outliers had to be flagged and manually parsed. This is no issue--as long as the scraper can flag them accurately. I iterated on a few crawling models to cover as many edge cases as possible. If the dataset had been larger, this method would have been unsustainable.

UbuWeb's emphasis on fluidity and transience prompted me to experiment with UbuTube's aesthetic structuration. I wanted the new design to reflect the original website's ideology in the same manner that its films do. The ideal, I thought, would be a website that rejects all conventions of web design and radically escapes towards other expressive modes.

The first draft took the form of a disparate arrangement of text boxes vying for space upon an undifferentiated white plane. The reasoning behind this deconstruction was to promote the hegemony of the filmic content over the non-filmic digital container. The negation of the container, however, does not remove the container. Like an inverted glove, negation relegates the content to the container's negative. This difficult loop prompted the exploration of other avenues of escape.

srcs.caption: First iteration of an UbuTube film page.

description: Instead of negating the container, we transform it. UbuTube becomes a Cahiers du Cinéma in miniature, a mimesis of print media lacking a target for its mimicry. The typography is totally uniform. Dividing borders demarcate coassociative textual zones like newspaper classifieds. The fixed outer margin suggests another medium: UbuTube is not a website, but rather a kind of pamphlet to be flipped through. The page-like navigation animations on the mobile interface are the most explicit expression of this.

As in a periodical, UbuTube's table of contents is brought to the fore, ever-present on the right-hand side of the page. Given the archive's sorting and filtering capacities, any one of UbuTube's 3000+ films is quickly and readily accessible from any other. Everything the user might need is available to them at any moment, but what the user actually wants--the film itself--constantly occupies the horizon of the gaze.

There are no images on the UbuTube website, save for two. The home page features a large reproduction of Kazimir Malevich's Black Square, while a small spiral--reproduced in the favicon--occupies the top left corner.

Malevich intended to separate art from imitation by neglecting artistic content and pursuing a radical supremacy of form. However, this dispossession inadvertently gave rise to a new kind of content synonymous with its own expression. Black Square is replete with content, but it is not symbolicating. Like a black hole collapsing on itself, what the painting is becomes inseparable from what it does.

Given the way that UbuWeb's films follow the avant-gardist tradition, I felt that it would be proper for UbuTube to do the same. Each film conntains its own preexisting array of content and expression, but when placed within the context of UbuTube, these layers fold into a singular content for which the site itself becomes the principal expressive medium. Instead of subjugating the content to the medium, we do the opposite: the site's expressive form becomes subjugated to its content, achieving a teleologically identical kind of synthesis. Everything is now directed towards the film, which sucks in the gaze of the user like the black hole of the black square.

UbuTube's minor symbol is the spiral (gidouille), which is a direct allusion to Alfred Jarry's Ubu Roi (1896). The gidouille adorns the stomach of Jarry's protagonist, representing his boundless hunger and greed. The spiral logomark was chosen for its metonomy with UbuWeb/Tube. A 1965 television adaptation of Ubu Roi is viewable on both sites.

srcs.caption: Black Square on display at the Tate Modern.[3]

description: Beyond visual changes, UbuTube's most marked divergence from UbuWeb involves its account system. UbuWeb has no user interactivity--but why would it need it? Account creation runs against its rhetoric of anonymity and impermanence. Regardless, the addition of users to UbuTube is a decision rooted more in pragmatics than ideology. UbuTube adds three principal features, each with its own logic:

1. Bookmarking: a user may bookmark films and return to them later via their profile. This gives the user motivation to explore the site, building their personal catalogue as they go. An individual film's bookmark count isn't displayed, so bookmarks don't function as 'likes', and bookmarking is not necessarily an indication of endorsement.

2. Commenting: unlike bookmarks, comments are displayed both on the pages of individual films and on the profiles of their authors. I was unsure whether including this feature would be the correct choice--I didn't want to present UbuTube as a social media platform. However, there are many platforms where comments are treated like 'reviews' and promote a higher level of engagement with digital material. To lay to rest any concerns, every comment has a minimum word count requirement.

3. View count: this feature was included out of statistical curiosity. Without a recommender system, which films would draw the most views? The answer turned out to be the films closest to the beginning of the catalog.

srcs.caption: Users are discouraged from making low-quality comments.
Bookmarks displayed on a user's page.

description: UbuTube now operates as a robust, efficient, and highly functional extension of UbuWeb.

The site's release had a tertiary effect that I had only vaguely considered during its development: by recreating UbuWeb, I was inadvertently bringing its films to a new demographic of internet users. Those who may not have been familiar with the original site now have the chance to easily explore and interact with its content. Although the avant-garde is sometimes regarded as strange or obtuse, I'm confident that, given the proper motivation, any individual has the capacity to appreciate it in the same way that they appreciate 'conventional' cinema. Only, it takes actions like these to lead them down that path.

items.title: arena flow
items.date: An infinite canvas data visualization program for Are.na.

description: Are.na is a content aggregation website geared towards artists, designers, and the curatorially-minded. It allows users to create 'blocks' and 'channels'. Blocks contain files uploaded by users, while channels are collections of those blocks (which may also contain channels themselves).

Since blocks can be shared between channels and appropriated by different users, the invisible web of connections quickly grows beyond the scope of Are.na's native UI. In order to apprehend Are.na's true complexity, I created arena flow, a web app that uses graph theory to dynamically construct directed graphs based on connections between blocks, channels, users, and groups.

The crucial insight behind arena flow was that Are.na shares key traits with a directed graph. When stripped down to its structural essence, the four types of Are.na objects (blocks, channels, users, and groups) are verticies, while the connections between them are edges. For instance, a channel C containing a block B can be represented by a directed edge from vertex C to vertex B. A block B owned by a user U can be represented likewise.

To algorithmically translate Are.na to a graph, I developed a custom graph engine that maintains adjacency lists of Are.na nodes, efficiently tracking and updating new connections as the user creates and removes them. This required two additional layers: a visual layer above for the user to interact with, and a network layer below to sync data with Are.na itself.

For the visual layer, I utilized React Flow, a React.js library that transforms the page into a draggable canvas. While the library was easy to set up, I found it didn't support all the operations that my engine required, so I modified it pragmatically as I developed the engine.

For the network layer, I made full use of the Are.na developer API to fetch and process Are.na data. The goal was to allow users of arena flow to do anything there that they'd be able to do on Are.na.
Together, these three layers work hand-over-hand to perform read, write, and update operations on actual Are.na blocks.

srcs.caption: Representation of Are.na neighborhood associativity. Users [U] create blocks [B] and channels [C]. Channels may contain blocks and other channels.
The principal layers of the arena flow client.

description: arena flow's user interface takes strong cues from the original Are.na design. Its gray-on-gray color scheme and emphasis on right angles accentuate and promote its actual content.

As with the original site, media blocks on arena flow are meant to be visually distinct from their backdrop. Unlike Are.na, however, there is no hierachical separation between blocks and channels. Everything is represented as an equal-sized block upon the canvas, and the user doesn't need to navigate between multiple pages to traverse connections.

srcs.caption: Side-by-side comparison of a channel on Are.na and its subsequent representation on arena flow.

description: This level of consistency gave rise to a problem: given the single-page layout and the large amount of data associated with each node, information can easily clutter the interface. To remediate this, I relegated everything to a collapsible pane on the left side of the canvas. The content of the pane is tied to the currently selected node. Crucially, a node's connected nodes can be added and removed from the canvas via the pane. The interaction between the information pane and the canvas constitutes arena flow's primary user loop.

The pane takes on a different layout based on the type of the selected node. Block nodes display block content and parent channels, channel nodes display channel children, and user nodes display a user's followers, following, and children. Another navigation pane occupies the top right of the canvas, displaying the logged-in user and a list of currently rendered nodes.

srcs.caption: Smooth transitions between panel/canvas states ensure an uninterrupted interaction loop.

description: During the first stage of its development, arena flow was functionally an Are.na renderer. It only had reading capabilities--changes on Are.na would affect the app, but changes on the app wouldn't write to Are.na. To take it to the next level, I realized that user actions on arena flow would have to be reflected on the parent site--otherwise, it would feel impermanent.

Fortunately, Are.na's API provides OAuth verification for 3rd-party clients. Using this, I set up a secure system where users could log in to create new blocks and channels using the canvas interface. By exploring the graph, they'd be able to add new blocks to their own channels, mimicking Are.na's content discovery flow.

The one shortcoming of this writing system was its failure to facilitate block/channel deletion. Unlike block creation/modification, which only requires a parent channel ID, Are.na block/channel deletion from third party applications requires knowledge of a special connection ID between the parent channel and the deletion target. Because the system I'd built didn't log official connection IDs and instead used a custom relationary schema, implementing deletion would have required a total refactor. If I'd known this from the beginning, I would have made the arena flow graph engine operate around connection IDs instead of node IDs.

srcs.caption: Logged-in user blocks (left) vs. non logged-in user blocks (right).
Logging in to an Are.na account through arena flow.
Utilizing OAuth login for block creation.
